name: Azure Kubernetes Service
summary: Microsoft’s managed Kubernetes: a control plane that can be free, node pools of Azure VMs, and an Automatic mode that runs the nodes too.
intro: When you create an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster, Azure creates and runs the control plane for you, and in a region with availability zones it spreads it over several zones by default. Your applications run on worker nodes grouped into node pools, usually backed by Virtual Machine Scale Sets in a separate node resource group in your subscription. Every cluster has a system node pool for critical Pods such as CoreDNS; you add user node pools for applications with different VM sizes, operating systems (Ubuntu by default, Azure Linux or Windows Server) or GPUs, and scale each pool by hand, with the cluster autoscaler, or with node autoprovisioning, which runs Karpenter for you. For untrusted code, Pod Sandboxing uses Kata Containers on Azure Linux nodes to run each Pod in a lightweight VM with its own guest kernel.

What you pay for the control plane depends on the tier. The Free tier charges nothing for it but has no SLA and is meant for clusters under about 10 nodes. The Standard tier adds a financially backed API server SLA and room for 5,000 nodes. The Premium tier adds Long Term Support, which keeps a Kubernetes version patched for two years in total, a year beyond the community support window. AKS Automatic, generally available since August 2025, is a preset cluster type on the Standard tier: Azure manages the system node pool, provisions nodes from Pod requests, and turns on Cilium-based networking, managed NGINX ingress, autoscalers and policy safeguards from the start.
strengths: A free control plane tier for development and small clusters, with a paid SLA one setting away
Long Term Support keeps one Kubernetes minor version patched for two years on the Premium tier
Several node pools per cluster, including Windows Server and GPU pools, each with its own VM size and OS
AKS Automatic gives a production baseline (node autoprovisioning, Cilium networking, ingress, safeguards) with one flag
limits: The Free tier has no SLA and isn’t meant for more than about 10 nodes; production clusters need Standard at $0.10 per cluster per hour
AKS supports only the three newest minor versions (N-2); staying longer means paying $0.60 per hour for Premium
AKS Automatic costs $0.16 per cluster per hour plus a per-vCPU management charge on its nodes, and gives up some node-level control
New AKS Automatic clusters can be created only in regions where API Server VNet Integration is generally available

snippet.title: Create a Standard-tier cluster and add a second node pool, or one Automatic cluster
source: az aks create --resource-group rg --name prod --tier standard \
# a user node pool for applications, with its own VM size and OS
az aks nodepool add --resource-group rg --cluster-name prod --name apps \
# or let Azure run the nodes as well
az aks create --resource-group rg --name auto --sku automatic

story: Microsoft’s first container service, Azure Container Service (ACS), launched in 2015 as a deployment engine for several open-source orchestrators, such as Docker Enterprise, Mesosphere DC/OS and Kubernetes. By October 2017 Kubernetes had pulled ahead: Microsoft said its use on ACS had grown 300% in six months.

On October 24, 2017, Microsoft announced a preview of AKS, a managed service focused only on Kubernetes, and promised that “you will pay nothing for the management of your Kubernetes cluster, ever”, while other clouds charged by the hour. AKS became generally available on June 13, 2018, in ten regions, announced by Brendan Burns, a Kubernetes co-founder who had moved from Google to Microsoft. Customers on the old service had to move to AKS by January 31, 2020.

AKS kept the free control plane as its Free tier but added paid ones: a Standard tier with an SLA for production, and a Premium tier with two-year Long Term Support. In August 2025 it made AKS Automatic generally available, a cluster type where Azure also manages the nodes using node autoprovisioning built on Karpenter, with billing starting in October 2025.

choices.choice: Kubernetes only, not a menu of orchestrators
choices.why: ACS supported several orchestrators. Microsoft said Kubernetes had “emerged as the open source standard for container orchestration”, so AKS focused its managed features on Kubernetes alone.

Microsoft argued that customers should pay only for the VMs that run their applications, not for the management infrastructure. That later became the Free tier, with SLAs and longer support sold as paid tiers on top.
Keeping critical Pods such as CoreDNS on their own pool stops a busy or misconfigured application pool from taking down the cluster’s own services.
Rather than write its own node provisioner, AKS adopted the open-source Karpenter and an Azure provider for it, so nodes are chosen from waiting Pods’ requests instead of fixed pool sizes.
